column2: Your first site made money. Your tenth is losing it. Same menu. Same brand. What changed?
It's unit economics: what one site earns after paying for itself. Sales, minus food, labour, rent and running costs. What's left is four-wall profit.
Here's site one. Twenty thousand pounds a week. Food takes twenty-eight percent, labour twenty-eight, rent ten, running costs ten. Four-wall profit: four thousand eight hundred pounds a week.

Now site ten. Weaker pitch, higher rent, sales of thirteen thousand. Food creeps to thirty percent with more waste. Here's the trap: labour barely moves. You still need a full team to open the doors. Labour hits forty percent. Site ten loses three hundred pounds a week.

Rent and labour are mostly fixed. When sales fall, they don't. Site ten needs about thirteen and a half thousand a week just to break even. A weaker site doesn't just earn a little less. It can lose money.
Site one's numbers don't predict site ten's. Model every new site on its own sales, with its own fixed costs.
Your question for Monday: what weekly sales does each of your sites need to break even?
